title: Quantum differential machine learning
abstract_summary: This preprint introduces Quantum Differential Machine Learning (QDML), a quantum analogue of classical differential machine learning that uses parameter-shift rules in parameterized quantum circuits to learn option prices and compute sensitivities (Greeks) efficiently. The paper demonstrates the approach on examples including European option deltas, Bermudan swaption vegas, and basket option deltas, highlighting benefits of overparameterization and potential speedups via parallel circuit evaluations.
methodology_description: The paper proposes Quantum Differential Machine Learning (QDML), a hybrid quantum-classical approach that uses parameterized quantum circuits (variational circuits) together with parameter-shift rules and chain-rule differentiation to learn option prices and their sensitivities (deltas, vegas). Inputs (market or path variables) are encoded into qubits via repeated data-reuploading RY/RZ rotations; trainable circuit blocks (built from optimal two-qubit building blocks UO with CNOTs and rotations) form the variational ansatz. Gradients with respect to circuit parameters and with respect to input-encoding parameters are computed exactly via parameter-shift rules; these analytic derivatives are combined with classical chain rules to recover sensitivities with respect to market variables. Training minimizes a loss that combines price-error and sensitivity-error terms with a weighting factor w. Different circuit sizes and parameterizations (including an overparameterized variant) are evaluated on three tasks: European call (2-qubit circuit, analytic Black–Scholes target), Bermudan swaption (4-qubit circuit built from 2-qubit blocks, targets generated by least-squares Monte Carlo under a Hull–White short-rate model), and a 7-asset basket option (6-qubit circuit, training on Monte Carlo pathwise payoffs under a Bachelier Gaussian model). Classical optimizers (Adam or AdaBelief) run the parameter updates, and parameter-shift evaluations (f(ϕ ± π/2) etc.) are used to compute both parameter gradients and input-output partials for sensitivities. Experiments were executed on classical simulators using Pennylane and PyTorch; no real quantum hardware was used.
algorithms_used: Least-Squares Monte Carlo (Longstaff-Schwartz) for Bermudan pricing
experimental_setup: All numerical experiments were performed on classical simulators (Pennylane-based quantum circuit simulators). No quantum hardware (QPU) was used. Classical Monte Carlo/LSMC simulations were used to generate training/benchmark data where relevant.
dataset_used: Three synthetic/ model-generated datasets were used: (1) European call prices: 20 training Black–Scholes call prices with spots spaced between 93 and 107 (K=100, T=0.25, σ=0.15) and 10 test spots; (2) Bermudan swaption: 201 training and 50 test instances; inputs are 9-dimensional (no-call period, tenor, 7 ATM normal volatilities) with vol matrix shifts; prices generated with a one-factor Hull–White short-rate model using least-squares Monte Carlo with 1,000,000 Monte Carlo simulations; (3) Basket option: simulated dataset from Bachelier Gaussian model for 7 correlated stocks (training size 8192, test size 4096) sourced from a Differential Machine Learning Jupyter notebook repository.

European.preprocessing: Prices and spots scaled into (0,1) via tanh-based transforms: x(S)=tanh((S/C1)^β) with C1=100,β=5; y(V)=tanh((V/C2)^γ) with C2=10,γ=0.75; encodings ϕj = arccos(x).

Bermudan.source: Monte Carlo / Least-Squares Monte Carlo under Hull–White model
Bermudan.preprocessing: Volatilities and tenor/no-call inputs transformed via tanh and aggregated into ϕ parameters (examples: t1 = tanh(sqrt(npc)/10), x(σ)=tanh(100σ)); groups of volatilities encoded together to reduce parameter-shift calls.

Basket.source: Simulated under Bachelier Gaussian model (DML repository notebook)
Basket.preprocessing: Inputs scaled with tanh (xi,j = tanh(Si,j / 6), yi = tanh(Vi)); encodings ϕ(x)=arccos(x) applied; pathwise deltas computed for training when provided.

common_steps: Encode preprocessed inputs into qubits via RY (and occasional RZ) rotations; use data-reuploading (multiple Uin(Φ) blocks interleaved with parameterized UP(Θ) blocks).
Construct variational ansatz: use optimal two-qubit construction UO(Θ) (15 parameters) as building block; compose to form 2-, 4- and 6-qubit circuits (specific architectures per experiment).
Define loss as weighted sum of price MSE and sensitivity MSE (weight w); normalize loss terms by target magnitude.

Compute circuit outputs f(Θ,Φ) and obtain analytic partial derivatives w.r.t. trainable parameters and input-encoding parameters via parameter-shift rules (f(ϕ±π/2) evaluations) and apply chain rule to map to market-variable sensitivities (delta/vega).
Optimize trainable parameters with a classical optimizer (Adam or AdaBelief) using computed gradients.

European_specifics.circuit: 2-qubit circuit with Uin(Φ) encoding inputs and UP(Θ)=UO(Θ) (15 parameters)
European_specifics.loss: MSE on price; optional added MSE term on delta with weight w

Bermudan_specifics.targets: Prices from LSMC; finite-difference vegas used as benchmark
Bermudan_specifics.loss: Weighted combination of price and parallel-vega errors (w parameter)

Basket_specifics.targets: Monte Carlo pathwise payoffs and pathwise deltas
Basket_specifics.loss: Weighted price MSE plus per-asset sensitivity MSE terms (weights wj normalized by average gradient magnitude)

key_findings: [supported] The paper introduces Quantum Differential Machine Learning (QDML), a quantum analogue of differential machine learning that uses parameter-shift rules to learn option prices and their sensitivities simultaneously.

[supported] Parameter-shift rules enable exact (analytical) gradient computation for parametrized quantum circuits and can be applied both to circuit parameters and to input-encoding parameters to obtain sensitivities.

[supported] On a simulator, a 2-qubit parametrized quantum circuit learned Black–Scholes European call prices with mean relative price error ≈0.069% and mean relative delta error ≈0.258% for the reported test set.

[supported] For a Bermudan swaption learning task (4-qubit circuits), overparameterization improved prediction robustness; without vega training the average tenor-normalized absolute vega error was large (~24.8% for NOP, ~26.2% for OP), while including vega in training reduced errors to ~6.2% (NOP) and ~4.6% (OP).

[supported] For a basket option learning task (6-qubit circuit) trained on Monte Carlo sample payoffs, adding pathwise delta information to the loss did not materially improve price estimation but did improve delta estimation.
[supported] All numerical experiments in the paper were performed on simulators rather than real quantum hardware.

[speculative] Parallel execution of multiple quantum circuits (one per parameter-shift evaluation) could substantially reduce wall-clock time for computing sensitivities if hardware supports that scale of parallelism.

[supported] Overparameterization (adding more circuit parameters / depth) is a useful strategy in quantum circuit learning for improving fit on more nonlinear/exotic payoffs, analogous to observations in classical deep learning.
[supported] Barren plateaus (vanishing gradients) are an important potential limitation as circuit size/depth increases; the paper notes the need for caution when scaling up.

[speculative] The paper suggests QDML could 'pave the way' for quantum machine learning applications in option pricing and sensitivity computation, but does not demonstrate a practical quantum advantage over classical methods.

[speculative] The paper cites literature claiming large energy-efficiency advantages for quantum computation relative to classical supercomputers and suggests quantum approaches could reduce electricity/CO2 for finance workloads; this is presented as a prospective benefit rather than an empirically demonstrated outcome within the paper.
results_summary: The authors propose QDML, leveraging parameter-shift rules in parametrized quantum circuits to learn option prices and sensitivities. Through simulator-based experiments they demonstrate that small circuits (2 qubits) can accurately learn European option prices and deltas, while more complex derivatives (Bermudan swaptions) benefit from overparameterization and inclusion of sensitivity data in training to reduce vega errors. A 6-qubit circuit trained on Monte Carlo sample payoffs showed that adding pathwise delta targets improves delta estimates but not price estimates. All results were obtained on simulators; practical speedups or hardware advantages remain prospective.
performance_claims: European call (2-qubit circuit, simulator): mean relative price error = 0.069%, mean relative delta error = 0.258% on the reported test set.

Bermudan swaption (4-qubit circuits): without vega training average tenor-normalized absolute vega error ≈ 24.8% (NOP) and ≈ 26.2% (OP); with vega included in training errors reduced to ≈ 6.2% (NOP) and ≈ 4.6% (OP).

Basket option (6-qubit circuit, training on Monte Carlo sample payoffs): training set size = 8192, test size = 4096; including sample-path deltas in the loss improved delta estimates but did not materially improve price estimates (specific numeric error changes reported in paper figures/tables).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper demonstrates feasibility of using parametrized quantum circuits and parameter-shift rules to learn prices and sensitivities on simulators, but does not provide evidence of a practical quantum advantage over classical methods. Claims about energy-efficiency or speedups are referenced from other literature and presented as prospective benefits contingent on future hardware capabilities (parallel execution, scalable quantum devices).
limitations: Quantum hardware immaturity: the experiments and methods are developed assuming near-term/idealized devices while practical, large-scale quantum hardware is still under development.
All numerical experiments were performed on simulators rather than real quantum hardware, so effects of noise, decoherence, and real device constraints are not evaluated.

Difficulty learning highly nonlinear/exotic products: Bermudan swaption prices and sensitivities are harder to learn accurately than simpler derivatives (e.g., European options); nonlinearity degrades performance unless mitigated (e.g., via overparameterization).
Unknown/ non-optimal multi-qubit ansatz: optimal constructions for SU(2^n) for more than two qubits remain unknown, so the paper uses composed two-qubit blocks which may be suboptimal.
Computational cost of sensitivity evaluation: parameter-shift rules require multiple circuit evaluations per partial derivative; sequential evaluation can be time-consuming.
Risk of barren plateaus: as parametrized circuit size increases gradients can vanish exponentially, limiting trainability of larger circuits.

Cost of generating training data for exotic options: true prices and sensitivities (from Monte Carlo/LSMC) are expensive to compute, motivating use of sample-space training but introducing noise and variance.
Limited scale of experiments: demonstrated circuits use small numbers of qubits (2, 4, 6) and low-dimensional inputs; scalability to high-dimensional, real-market problems is untested.
[inferred] Lack of evaluation under realistic hardware noise and finite sampling — impact on gradient estimation (parameter-shift) and optimization stability is unknown.
[inferred] Encoding restrictions: parameter-shift applicability assumes specific parametric gate forms (e^{-i a phi G}), which may constrain data-encoding choices and model expressivity.

[inferred] Parallel execution requirement: efficient sensitivity computation in practice may require parallel execution of many circuits, which depends on hardware capabilities that may not be available.
[inferred] Unclear generalization / overfitting trade-offs for overparameterized quantum circuits when trained on noisy or limited financial datasets.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — QDML proposes that analytic parameter-shift differentiation of variational circuits plus parallel circuit evaluations can yield speedups for computing option prices and Greeks compared to naive classical finite-difference approaches.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The method is hybrid: parameterized quantum circuits (data-reuploading ansatz) provide outputs and analytic partials via parameter-shift rules, while classical chain-rule differentiation and classical optimizers (Adam/AdaBelief) handle training and mapping to market-variable sensitivities.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Designed as a NISQ-compatible approach using overparameterized variational ansätze and data-reuploading; demonstrated on small-scale 2-, 4-, and 6-qubit circuits for European, Bermudan, and multi-asset basket examples.

#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments were run on classical simulators (Pennylane + PyTorch); no experiments on real quantum hardware, so hardware performance and noise effects are not assessed.

#limitation:data-encoding — Uses repeated data-reuploading and arccos/tanh preprocessing; parameter-shift gradients require many circuit evaluations and the paper groups inputs to reduce calls, indicating nontrivial encoding and evaluation cost.

#limitation:qubit-count — Demonstrations are limited to small qubit counts (2–6 qubits) on synthetic/model-generated datasets; scalability to production-size, high-dimensional derivatives is untested.
